cases.ratio: Implementing an international arbitral award that merely settles a disputed/undefined boundary (as opposed to ceding defined Indian territory to a foreign state) does not require a constitutional amendment under Article 368 or legislation under Article 3, and can be given effect to by the Union executive under Article 253/73; cession of clearly Indian territory, by contrast, does require a constitutional amendment.
cases.kanoonQuery: Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1970) 3 SCC 400

cases.name: In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves
cases.ratio: Answering a Presidential reference under Article 143, an eight-judge bench held that implementing the India-Pakistan agreement to transfer the Berubari Union and exchange enclaves amounts to cession of Indian territory, which cannot be done merely by ordinary legislation under Article 3; it requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368. The Court also observed, in passing, that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution and is not by itself a source of substantive power (a view later revisited by Kesavananda Bharati, which held the Preamble is part of the Constitution and reflects its basic structure).
cases.kanoonQuery: In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves AIR 1960 SC 845

cases.name: Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay
cases.ratio: The proviso to Article 3 requires that a State Legislature be given the opportunity to express its views on a Bill affecting its area/boundaries as originally introduced, but if Parliament later amends the Bill, there is no further constitutional requirement to send it back to the State Legislature for fresh views on the amended proposal; the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 was accordingly upheld as validly enacted.
cases.kanoonQuery: Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay AIR 1960 SC 51

cases.name: Mangal Singh v. Union of India
cases.ratio: Parliament's power under Article 3 to form a new State or alter boundaries includes ancillary power under Article 4 to make supplemental and incidental provisions -- including giving the new States of Punjab and Haryana different legislative structures (bicameral and unicameral respectively) -- and such incidental provisions in a reorganisation Act are not open to challenge merely because they create some difference in the new States' constitutional setup.
cases.kanoonQuery: Mangal Singh v. Union of India AIR 1967 SC 944

cases.name: Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India
cases.ratio: The Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act, 1983, which applied only to Assam and made it disproportionately difficult to identify and deport illegal migrants compared to the Foreigners Act, 1946 applicable elsewhere, was struck down as unconstitutional; the influx of illegal migrants into Assam was held to constitute 'external aggression and internal disturbance' under Article 355, casting a duty on the Union to protect the State, which the IMDT Act's weak procedure defeated.
cases.kanoonQuery: Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005) 5 SCC 665

cases.name: Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan
cases.ratio: A tax that is compensatory or regulatory in nature -- that is, one that is a fair recompense for the use of facilities like roads that the State provides to traders and carriers -- does not amount to a restriction on the freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse under Article 301, even without complying with the safeguards in Article 304(b); the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act was upheld on this basis. (Note: the separate 'compensatory tax' category this case created was later overruled by the nine-judge Jindal Stainless bench in 2016, which held ordinary non-discriminatory taxation does not need to meet a special compensatory test at all.)
cases.kanoonQuery: Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan AIR 1962 SC 1406

cases.name: Atiabari Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam
cases.ratio: A tax that directly and immediately restricts the free movement of trade, commerce and intercourse across State lines -- here, a tax on goods carried by road or inland waterway, levied simply because the goods crossed the State -- falls within Article 301's guarantee and is invalid unless it satisfies Article 304(b)'s conditions (previous Presidential sanction and reasonableness); a tax that only indirectly or remotely affects trade is not caught by Article 301.
cases.kanoonQuery: Atiabari Tea Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam AIR 1961 SC 232

cases.name: Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana
cases.ratio: A nine-judge bench overruled the 'compensatory tax' doctrine created in Atiabari and Automobile Transport: a non-discriminatory tax (such as an entry tax on goods brought from other States, so long as it does not discriminate against imported goods in favour of similar local goods) does not per se violate Article 301, and States need not separately prove the tax is compensatory to justify it; Article 304(a) permits such non-discriminatory taxation without the Article 304(b)/Presidential-sanction route.
cases.kanoonQuery: Jindal Stainless Ltd. v. State of Haryana (2017) 12 SCC 1

cases.name: Bhikraj Jaipuria v. Union of India
cases.ratio: A contract made on behalf of the Government must comply with the formal requirements now in Article 299(1) -- expressed to be made in the name of the President/Governor and executed by a duly authorised person -- and a contract that does not comply with these mandatory formalities is not enforceable against the Government, even if the Government has in substance agreed to its terms.
cases.kanoonQuery: Bhikraj Jaipuria v. Union of India AIR 1962 SC 113

cases.name: State of Rajasthan v. Vidhyawati
cases.ratio: The State is vicariously liable, like any other employer, for the tortious acts of its servants committed in the course of and incidental to their employment -- here, a government driver's negligent driving of an official jeep -- even though the old immunity for acts done in exercise of 'sovereign functions' inherited from the East India Company era might otherwise have been claimed; Article 300 allows the State to be sued in the same manner as it could have been before the Constitution, subject to this ordinary vicarious liability.
cases.kanoonQuery: State of Rajasthan v. Vidhyawati AIR 1962 SC 933

cases.name: Kasturilal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.ratio: The State is not liable in tort for the negligence of its police officers where the negligent act (here, misappropriation of goods seized and held in police custody) was done in the exercise of a sovereign function -- the power of arrest and seizure -- even though the individual officers may be personally liable; this narrower sovereign-immunity exception has been much criticised and increasingly confined in later cases, but Kasturilal itself was never formally overruled.
cases.kanoonQuery: Kasturilal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1965 SC 1039

cases.name: Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat
cases.ratio: The right to property under Article 300A is only a constitutional/legal right, not a fundamental right and not part of the basic structure; a person can be deprived of property only by authority of a validly enacted law, but once such a law exists and is followed, the adequacy of compensation is not open to the same judicial scrutiny as it would be for a fundamental right.
cases.kanoonQuery: Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat 1995 Supp (1) SCC 596

cases.name: K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka
cases.ratio: Even though Article 300A does not guarantee a fixed quantum of compensation as a fundamental right, a law depriving a person of property must still provide for some determination of compensation through a fair and reasonable procedure and cannot be arbitrary or illusory; total exclusion of any right to compensation or an utterly whimsical amount could render the deprivation unconstitutional as violating Article 14 or the rule of law, even where Article 300A itself is satisfied.
cases.kanoonQuery: K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011) 9 SCC 1

cases.name: Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh
cases.ratio: The State cannot take possession of a citizen's land for a public purpose (here, road construction) for decades without initiating formal acquisition proceedings or paying compensation, and cannot rely on adverse possession to defeat the owner's title; such a taking without following due process violates Article 300A (and implicates Article 21's due-process guarantee), and the right to property, though no longer a fundamental right, remains a basic human and constitutional right.
cases.kanoonQuery: Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020) 2 SCC 569

cases.name: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel
cases.ratio: The second proviso to Article 311(2), added by the 42nd Amendment, validly dispenses with the ordinary requirement of a disciplinary inquiry before dismissal, removal or reduction in rank in three defined situations -- conviction on a criminal charge, where it is not reasonably practicable to hold an inquiry, or where the President/Governor is satisfied that holding one is not expedient in the interest of State security; these exceptions do not violate natural justice as a constitutional matter because Article 311(2) itself carves them out.
cases.kanoonQuery: Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel (1985) 3 SCC 398

cases.name: Parshotam Lal Dhingra v. Union of India
cases.ratio: Whether an order terminating or reverting a government servant attracts the protection of Article 311(2) depends not on its form but on whether it is founded on misconduct and visits the servant with evil consequences (a punitive dismissal/removal/reduction in rank), or is a bona fide exercise of an ordinary power such as termination during probation or reversion from an officiating post, which does not require a prior inquiry even though it may incidentally cause loss of the higher post.
cases.kanoonQuery: Parshotam Lal Dhingra v. Union of India AIR 1958 SC 36

cases.name: Ashok Kumar Yadav v. State of Haryana
cases.ratio: A Public Service Commission's assessment of candidates at a viva voce interview under Article 320 is not ordinarily open to judicial review merely because the marks allotted seem low, and will be interfered with only if the assessment is patently arbitrary; the Court also recommended, as good practice, that the number of candidates called for interview after a written exam should not exceed twice or thrice the number of vacancies, to keep the interview's weight in proportion.
cases.kanoonQuery: Ashok Kumar Yadav v. State of Haryana (1985) 4 SCC 417

cases.name: Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner
cases.ratio: Article 324 vests the Election Commission with wide residuary power to take all necessary steps -- including cancelling a poll and ordering a fresh one -- to ensure free and fair elections, in situations not expressly covered by the Representation of the People Act or rules made under it, so long as the power is exercised in good faith and consistently with the Act's provisions rather than in conflict with them.
cases.kanoonQuery: Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978) 1 SCC 405

cases.name: Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India
cases.ratio: Until Parliament enacts a law under Article 324(2), the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners shall be appointed by the President on the advice of a committee comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition (or the leader of the largest opposition party) in the Lok Sabha, and the Chief Justice of India, so as to insulate the Election Commission's independence from unilateral executive control. (Note: Parliament subsequently enacted the CEC and Other ECs Act, 2023, replacing the CJI on the selection committee with a Union Cabinet Minister, which is itself under further constitutional challenge.)
cases.kanoonQuery: Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023) 6 SCC 161

cases.name: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (NOTA)
cases.ratio: The right to cast a negative vote by choosing 'None of the Above' (NOTA) is part of a voter's right to freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a), exercised through the electoral process under Article 326; the Election Commission was directed to provide a NOTA option on EVMs and ballot papers, while preserving the voter's right to secrecy about how they voted.
cases.kanoonQuery: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (NOTA) (2013) 10 SCC 1

cases.name: Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal
cases.ratio: The right to vote or stand for election is not a common-law or fundamental right but a special statutory right created by the Representation of the People Act, to be exercised strictly within the limits that Act sets; an election dispute is accordingly a creature of and confined to the statute, and non-candidate individuals (such as ministers impleaded in an election petition on allegations of corrupt practice) can be made parties only as the statute permits.
cases.kanoonQuery: Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal (1982) 1 SCC 691

cases.name: N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer, Namakkal
cases.ratio: Article 329(b) bars any court, including under Article 226, from interfering with an election -- including the wrongful rejection of a nomination paper -- while the election process is underway; the word 'election' is used in a wide sense covering the entire process from the notification of the election to the declaration of the result, and any grievance about that process must be raised only through an election petition after the election is over.
cases.kanoonQuery: N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer, Namakkal AIR 1952 SC 64

cases.name: Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister
cases.ratio: Maharashtra's law granting a separate 16% reservation to the Maratha community, over and above existing quotas, was struck down as unconstitutional for breaching the 50% ceiling from Indra Sawhney without any extraordinary circumstance justifying an exception; the Court also held that after the 102nd Amendment (inserting Articles 338B and 342A), only the President (through a notification, with Parliament able to amend the list) -- not the States -- can identify socially and educationally backward classes for the purposes of the Central list, though this holding on State power was later reversed by the 105th Amendment restoring States' power to maintain their own SEBC lists.
cases.kanoonQuery: Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister (2021) 8 SCC 1

cases.name: State of Maharashtra v. Milind
cases.ratio: Only communities specifically and expressly notified in the President's Order under Articles 341/342 (as later amended by Parliament) are recognised as Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes; courts, State authorities and tribunals cannot hold an inquiry to include a sub-caste or sub-tribe (such as 'Halba Koshti' under the notified 'Halba/Halbi' entry) that is not itself expressly named in the Order, however similar it may be to a notified community.
cases.kanoonQuery: State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2001) 1 SCC 4

cases.name: State of Karnataka v. Associated Management of English Medium Primary and Secondary Schools
cases.ratio: A State government order compelling all recognised primary schools to use the mother tongue or the regional language (Kannada) as the sole medium of instruction was struck down as unconstitutional; the choice of medium of instruction is part of the right of a student (through the parent) to receive information and express themselves under Article 19(1)(a), and of a linguistic minority's rights, and cannot be dictated by the State, though the State can regulate curriculum and standards.
cases.kanoonQuery: State of Karnataka v. Associated Management of English Medium Primary and Secondary Schools (2014) 9 SCC 485

cases.name: Makhan Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.ratio: A Presidential Order under Article 359 suspending the right to move any court for enforcement of specified fundamental rights (here, Articles 21 and 22) during a proclaimed Emergency bars a detenu from challenging their detention on the ground that it contravenes those specific rights, but does not bar a challenge on grounds outside the Order altogether, such as that the detaining authority acted mala fide, outside its statutory power, or under a law not made in good faith.
cases.kanoonQuery: Makhan Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1964 SC 381

cases.name: Sampat Prakash v. State of Jammu and Kashmir
cases.ratio: The power under Article 370(1) to apply provisions of the Constitution to Jammu and Kashmir with modifications, exercised through Presidential Orders, continues to be validly exercisable even after the State's Constituent Assembly (contemplated by the proviso to Article 370(3)) had dissolved; the Article did not become spent or inoperable merely because the body originally meant to be consulted no longer existed, since Article 370 itself remained part of the Constitution.
cases.kanoonQuery: Sampat Prakash v. State of Jammu and Kashmir AIR 1969 SC 1153

cases.name: In re Article 370 of the Constitution
cases.ratio: A five-judge Constitution Bench unanimously upheld the President's 2019 orders abrogating the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 and applying the entire Constitution of India to the former State; it held that Article 370 was always a temporary/transitional provision meant to facilitate integration, that the President could exercise the power under Article 370(3) even without the Constituent Assembly's concurrence once that body had ceased to exist, and it did not rule on the separate legal challenge to bifurcating the State into two Union Territories, treating that as a distinct issue.
cases.kanoonQuery: In re Article 370 of the Constitution 2023 INSC 1058

cases.name: Keshav Madhav Menon v. State of Bombay
cases.ratio: Article 13(1) operates prospectively: a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a fundamental right becomes void only from the date the Constitution commenced (26 January 1950) and only to the extent of the inconsistency, and does not retroactively wipe out things done, or proceedings validly initiated, under that law before the Constitution came into force; a criminal prosecution begun before that date under such a law could therefore continue.
cases.kanoonQuery: Keshav Madhav Menon v. State of Bombay AIR 1951 SC 128

cases.name: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.ratio: Established the doctrine of eclipse: a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a fundamental right is not wiped out but becomes unenforceable ('eclipsed') only against citizens to the extent of the inconsistency; if the relevant fundamental right is later removed or amended (here, by nationalising motor transport, taking the law's operation into a field no longer protected as a citizen's right), the law is freed from the shadow and becomes fully operative again without needing to be re-enacted.
cases.kanoonQuery: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh AIR 1955 SC 781

cases.name: Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh
cases.ratio: Government land, forest land and tribal-owned land in Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule cannot be leased to non-tribal persons or private companies for mining; such leases were declared null and void, and mining in these Scheduled Areas may be carried on only through State-run corporations or tribal cooperatives, in order to protect tribal ownership and self-governance over land as intended by the Fifth Schedule and Article 244.
cases.kanoonQuery: Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) 8 SCC 191

cases.name: Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre
cases.ratio: LIC, as a State instrumentality under Article 12, must exercise its power to frame insurance policy terms consistently with the constitutional goals of social and economic justice reflected in the Preamble and the Directive Principles; a policy condition (Table 58) that arbitrarily excluded persons not in organised-sector employment from a low-premium policy was struck down as unreasonable, discriminatory and violative of Article 14.
cases.kanoonQuery: Life Insurance Corporation of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995) 5 SCC 482

cases.name: Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.ratio: The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI), despite enjoying a de facto monopoly over cricket and performing functions with a public character, is not financially, functionally or administratively controlled by the government and is therefore not 'State' or 'other authority' under Article 12; it is not amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 32, though its public functions may still be challengeable before a High Court under the wider Article 226.
cases.kanoonQuery: Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of India (2005) 4 SCC 649

cases.name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges case)
cases.ratio: 'Consultation' with the Chief Justice of India under Articles 124 and 222 for judicial appointments and transfers does not mean 'concurrence'; the executive's view prevails in case of disagreement, giving the government primacy over the judiciary in appointments (a position overruled by the Second Judges case in 1993). The judgment separately liberalised locus standi, holding that any public-spirited citizen or group can invoke Article 32 on behalf of persons unable to approach the Court themselves, laying the foundation for public interest litigation in India.
cases.kanoonQuery: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges case) 1981 Supp SCC 87
